title: Engine Adapter Registry — Core Method
description: A federation manager never talks to engines directly; it talks to adapters, one per engine, that translate the canonical query into the engine's protocol and normalize its results back. The registry tracks each adapter's health, latency history, and supported features, probed on a schedule. An unhealthy adapter is quarantined automatically so one sick engine cannot poison the federation. This adapter layer is the difference between a federation manager and ad-hoc multi-search code: engines come and go, but the coordination logic never changes. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Quorum Aggregation — Core Method
description: Waiting for every engine means the slowest engine sets the pace, so the manager uses quorum aggregation: return as soon as k of n engines have answered. The quorum size balances completeness against latency — a majority quorum tolerates slow engines while still hearing most of the federation. Late arrivals are merged into the result set if they beat the deadline, otherwise logged and dropped. This is the same trade-off distributed databases make between consistency and availability, applied to search. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
import time
engines = {"a": 0.05, "b": 0.30, "c": 0.08}
K = 2
start = time.time()
done, order = [], sorted(engines, key=engines.get)
for name in order:
    time.sleep(engines[name])
    done.append(name)
    if len(done) >= K: break
print("quorum of %d reached with: %s (%.2fs)" % (K, done, time.time() - start))

title: Timeout and Fallback Policy — Core Method
description: Every engine gets a deadline derived from its latency history plus a safety margin, and anything slower is cut off rather than allowed to stall the federation. When an engine times out, the fallback policy decides: retry once, route its shard to a replica, or proceed without it and note the gap. Policies are configured per engine class — local indexes get tight deadlines, remote APIs get generous ones. Explicit timeouts turn unpredictable distributed behavior into predictable degraded behavior, which users vastly prefer to a hung search. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Protocol Translation Layer — Core Method
description: Engines speak different protocols — one takes JSON over HTTP, another takes SQL, a third takes a proprietary binary query — so the manager translates the canonical query into each dialect at dispatch time. Translation is declarative: a mapping table per engine converts canonical operators to native ones, and anything untranslatable is flagged before dispatch rather than failing mid-search. Result translation runs in reverse, normalizing scores and field names into the canonical result shape. Centralizing translation here means query logic is written once and works against every engine. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Cost-Aware Engine Selection — Core Method
description: Not every query needs every engine: a cost-aware manager estimates each engine's price in latency, compute, or API fees, and selects the cheapest subset that still covers the query's requirements. Coverage is checked against the capability registry, and the selection is re-evaluated per query because costs shift with load. Expensive engines are reserved for queries that genuinely need them, which keeps routine searches fast and cheap. This turns federation from a blunt broadcast into an economical, deliberate routing decision. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
